title: Opus5.5 Low to Max - Godot 4.7 vs Unreal 5.8
author: 314t
selftext:
These results were interesting. Claude performed worse on Low in Unreal than Godot, and completely skipped the rain in all Unreal scenes. Claude also tended to work long when developing in Unreal over Godot. What I observed that took up good chunks of these times were assets importing into Unreal, and rendering captures to review its own work, overall just engine overhead.

Overall, Claude took longer waiting around of Unreal, and spent more tokens working in Unreal, but do the results speak for themselves? Does one engine look better in your opinion? 

  
**Godot Prompt:**

Build a moody Godot 4 diorama: overgrown cyberpunk alley at blue hour, rain-slicked PBR surfaces, neon emissive signs with bloom, volumetric fog, SDFGI, ACES tonemapping, tilt-shift depth of field, scattered set dressing, low-angle hero shot.

  
**Unreal Prompt:**

Build a moody Unreal Engine 5 diorama: overgrown cyberpunk alley at blue hour, rain-slicked PBR surfaces, neon emissive signs with bloom, volumetric fog, Lumen global illumination, ACES tonemapping, tilt-shift depth of field, scattered set dressing, low-angle hero shot.

comments.author: 314t
comments.body:
Yes, each prompt is accompanied by these rules, sometimes I already have a 3d Asset downloaded from previous runes, so Claude just finds it in a shared library. Any downloaded or previously created assets get placed in the shared library, with a running catalog.

\## Working rules for this run

\- We are going to build a Godot/Unreal project, in this folder.

\- Run everything headless where possible.

\- Capture screenshots as needed to verify the visuals.

\- Use retrieved 3D assets (download free, properly licensed models, textures and HDRIs). Do not hand-roll assets: no hand-built procedural stand-ins for props or set dressing.

\- You are allowed 1 helper (subagent) at most.

\- \[my 3d library path\] may have existing assets you can reuse (see its library folder and its AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). Check there before downloading. Copy anything you use into this project; do not modify \[my 3d library path\].

replies.author: 314t
replies.body: Generally no, from my testing the agent will generally implement these on their own, but not 100% of the time, I specifically wanted these implemented so I asked for them. SDFGI without prompting, it would try to just use ambient light from the sky, its more of a polish to get real-time bounced lighting. The aces tonemapping works well for the neon lights. I have tested slightly differnt wording, and some words can drastically change a scene, and some have little or no impact. The aces tonemapping probably has the least impact.

replies.author: 314t
replies.body:
One giant scene in Godot. Claude is bad at this, and will constantly do this if you don't specify rules for structuring the game repo and scenes.

Shaders - it used many, for the wet ground, the sky color, tilt shift, neon lights, winows, mist, fog. Max used the most shaders,

Yes, it populated the scene with GDScript, it never does it with the node tree.

Unreal, similar to Godot, it populated the scene with C++ scripts at runtime, no usd.

Yes, fair enough, I did not specifiy rain in the prompt, but much of my simulations of specific words - 'moody' usually results in rain, which is why I found it interesting that not even one Unreal build got rain.

replies.author: 314t
replies.body:
First thing I do is have claude pull assets it thinks it will need into a shared library. It finds assets from the web, that are free license, that require or don't require attribution (e.g cc0/cc4). I tell it finding pre-made assets are preferable. As this point, the library I have is over 2k assets over the last few months, so claude most of the time finds what it needs.

When actually implementing a scene, I tell the agent to NEVER handroll assets. Because they will look like dog poo. We create assets in their own sessions, implementation in another.

To actually create assets it could not find, we start this in a new session and we start a workflow   
1. one agent researches the 3D model we want to create, can be medium effort. The research agent then gathers reference images and writes a FULL BRIEF / SPECIFICATION (shape, topology, uv, normals, textures, ao, etc.) that it will then hand off to a LOW opus agent. Its told specifically get reference images with good lighting, and any dark areas, they should try to find closeups with better lighting, else it will create non-sensical topology.  
2. the low OPUS agent builds it based off the brief and reference images.  
3. a CRITIC medium agent runs, tells the opus low agent if their work SUCKS.  
5. sent back for revision if anything bad

  
Obviously this is a little token heavy, so if you're not lazy like me, you can find the reference images yourself, and describe it, and focus on areas with complex shape and topology and try to really explain that in detail
